lesson_title: Measure the Sea From the Lighthouse
hook_text: 165 metres of open water, measured without leaving the tower. Two decisions. That's all.
clip_script: Stand at the top of a lighthouse and tilt down to a ship: the angle your gaze drops through is the angle of depression. And one beautiful fact rescues every confusing depression question: the angle you look down at the ship equals the angle the sailor looks up at you. Your level line and the sea are parallel, so the two angles must match. Move to the ship and look up twenty degrees instead. The lighthouse faces you — opposite, sixty. The sea runs beside you — adjacent, unknown. Tangent — but the unknown is downstairs, so divide: sixty over tangent twenty is one hundred and sixty-four comma eight five metres. A distance across open water, measured by someone who never left the tower.
visual_style: A lighthouse at dusk, a dotted horizontal line and a sight-line dropping to a small ship; the camera swoops to the ship as the matching angle glows, then the distance ticks out along the water in metres.
pacing: Slow establishing beat on the tower, a satisfying flip down to the ship, the number landing as the payoff.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for the ladder, the wire, the ramp and the eye-height trap.
